title: Permutations III
statement: Return every way to arrange the numbers `1` through `n`, each used exactly once, so that every two neighbouring numbers are one odd and one even. List the arrangements in lexicographic order: of two arrangements, the one with the smaller number at the first position where they differ comes first.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all `n!` orderings and filtering them works, but most of them break the parity rule early. Instead, build the arrangement one position at a time and refuse any number whose parity matches the number just placed, so only valid prefixes are extended. Since every position tries its candidates from `1` up to `n`, finished arrangements appear in lexicographic order and need no sorting.

## Approach

1. Keep the arrangement being built in `path`, mark placed numbers in `used`, and collect finished arrangements in `result`.
2. `backtrack()` first checks whether `path` holds all `n` numbers; if so it stores a copy and returns.
3. Otherwise it tries each `value` from 1 to `n`, skipping values already used and values with the same parity as the last number in `path`.
4. For an allowed `value`, mark it, push it, recurse, then pop it and unmark it so the next candidate starts from the same prefix.
5. Call `backtrack()` once on the empty path and return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

With `n = 4` the search places `1`, then needs an even number: `2`, then odd `3`, then even `4`, storing `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. Neither `[1, 2, 3]` nor `[1, 2]` can be finished another way, so it backs up to `[1]` and tries `4`, then `3`, then `2`: `[1, 4, 3, 2]`. Starting with `2` gives `[2, 1, 4, 3]` and `[2, 3, 4, 1]`, starting with `3` gives `[3, 2, 1, 4]` and `[3, 4, 1, 2]`, and starting with `4` gives `[4, 1, 2, 3]` and `[4, 3, 2, 1]`. The eight lists come out already sorted.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · P), where P is the number of valid arrangements (8 for `n = 4`, 2,880 for `n = 9`): each of the `n` levels holds at most P prefixes, and each prefix scans `n` candidates.
- Space: O(n) for `path`, `used` and the recursion, plus O(n · P) for the returned lists.

## Pitfalls

- Store a copy (`[...path]`), not `path` itself; otherwise every entry is the same array, which ends up empty.
- Undo both changes after the recursive call (`path.pop()` and `used[value] = false`), or later branches start from a wrong state.
- The first position has no neighbour to its left, so skip the parity test while `path` is empty.
- If you sort afterwards, the default `sort()` compares the lists as text (`10` before `2`); trying values in increasing order makes sorting unnecessary.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | finished arrangements, in lexicographic order |
| `path` | the arrangement being built |
| `used` | `used[v]` is true while `v` is in `path` |
| `backtrack` | fills the next position of `path` in every allowed way |
| `value` | the candidate number for the next position |
